newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Revolution brings new life to east Zairean city.
newsitem.headline: Revolution brings new life to east Zairean city.

text.p: Rebels toting Kalashnikovs guard the disc jockey's booth at Shushi's Nightclub and Limbo Lounge in the heart of Goma above the Pentecostal Church of Spiritual Combat.
Five rebels sport wrap-around sunglasses, the music is the jumping Zairean Lingala reggae of Papa Wemba and the club dance floor is packed with jubilant Zaireans most nights these days.
"This is the first dance since the revolution," shouts a young woman in sunglasses, swaying in front of the dance floor mirror, clutching a pair of white rubber surgical gloves.

A revolution since October led by Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels against President Mobutu Sese Seko and Zaire's ill-disciplined and rarely paid government army has changed the face of a swath of eastern Zaire.
Laurent Kabila, president of the rebel Democratic Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, has renamed the region, the rebel army and even the main river.
Eastern Zaire has become Democratic Congo, the rebel army has been renamed the Congolese Liberation Army (CLA), and the Zaire river flowing north has reverted to the name Congo.

In a letter sent this week to Mobutu, recovering at a luxury villa in France, Kabila accused the president of having been bent on the destruction "of this jubilant emblem of national pride, this charming, sweet and vast land of the Congo".
Exiled for 36 years, Kabila and his coalition of four other parties have reignited a sense of civic pride in rebel-held parts of the east, which suffered from years of neglect.
For many Zaireans in the 550 km (340-mile) stretch of rebel-held territory stretching from north to south, the revolution means liberation from the Zairean army and a chance to restart their lives.

Thomas Makafunzi weeded a roundabout in the centre of the city of Goma this week, one of hundreds of local people who are embracing a return of civic pride in what was for years a centre for gun law and extortion by soldiers.
"I had a choice between guarding a food warehouse with a stick, weeding roundabouts or edging verges. I got the weeding, but frankly I hoped to get edging," Makafunzi told Reuters.
Goma, a resort on the shores of Lake Kivu which fell into anarchy with the arrival of hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees in 1994, is now tidier than many European cities.
Its streets are swept clean of rubbish and volcanic dust, its shops are reopening, and potatoes, onions, dried fish, manioc flour and oil -- all staples -- are now readily available in its markets.
Petrol prices are steady at $1 per litre, and the currency is 80,000 rebel new zairoises to the dollar.
Money changers hover on its street corners with wads of new notes the size of housebricks in their hands.
"We don't know what to do about the currency," says Kabila's adviser Jean Kabongo. "The dollar is so good. It stops inflation and stops corrupt people going off and printing money."
The provinces of north and south Kivu are the breadbasket of Zaire, and as the rebels advance more food becomes available.
But behind military successes follow government problems.
"The liberated area has no government yet," noted Kabila this week. "It is just part of the country free from Mobutu."
Local Zairean aid workers, all unpaid volunteers, patrol the streets and nearby refugee camps, helping refugee stragglers, disinfecting sites of killing and removing decomposing corpses.
"We like to think that what is going on here is a Zairean solution to a Zairean problem," says Doctor Jo Lusi at Goma's Virunga hospital. "We can prove we can look after ourselves."
The refugee camps of Mugunga, Kibumba, Kahindo, Katale and Lac Vert to the northeast and northwest now lie empty. Three weeks ago they held more than 700,000 Rwandan refugees.
Small shelters built of volcanic rock are overgrown and the wind off volcanoes blows among debris. The ground is blooming with hundreds of daisies, gladioli, sunflowers and marigolds.

Only Zairean charcoal burners move among the ruins, taking wood. "Imagine finding this place in the future," says Freddy Moakata, a Zairean aid worker. "It would be like coming across a lost civiisation."
